newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung favourably reviews Fokker buyout terms.
newsitem.headline: Samsung favourably reviews Fokker buyout terms.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries hinted on Friday that a deal was within sight on a Dutch proposal to take over bankrupt airplane maker Fokker NV
"The Dutch government is demanding a $500-$600 million long-term investment in Fokker and we are favourably reviewing the proposal," a Samsung spokesman said.
"We are undertaking negotiations with the Dutch government in a very amicable, positive manner but no agreement has been reached yet," the spokesman said.
He denied a domestic newspaper report that Samsung had agreed in principle to take over Fokker for $150 million.
The Dutch government said it had no comment on the Samsung spokesman's remarks. "We are making no announcement on this," said Luuc van Zijp, a spokesman of the Dutch Economic Ministry.
He added that as far as he was aware, there was no news conference planned for Friday on the matter.
Samsung Aerospace, a unit of Samsung Group, wants to assemble aircraft developed by Fokker for sale in Asia, with the Dutch firm continuing to market for Europe, the Samsung spokesman said.
He said any agreement would be subject to approval by the Dutch parliament and the South Korean government.

Fokker was declared bankrupt on March 15 after majority shareholder Daimler Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler Benz AG, cut off financial aid, saying it was no longer able to bear Fokker's huge losses.

Since then Samsung Aerospace has emerged as the only serious candidate to revive Fokker's core plane-making operations. In September the administrators gave Samsung the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books with a view to a possible takeover bid.
Since its demise, Fokker has continued production of aircraft with some 650 assembly workers. It has even accepted new orders to help preserve the value of assets.
Analysts in Seoul said the market for mid-sized passenger planes was already crowded.

"It's very hard to predict future demand for mid-sized aircraft," said Nam Kwon-oh at Ssangyong Investment Securities. "But the success of the venture would depend heavily on securing markets, and that may not be easy."

Daniel Harwood, the Seoul-based regional director of HG Asia, agreed. "Everyone's looking at Asia as the fastest-growing area for the aeronautics business, be it little jets or regional airliners. But there's huge oversupply. What can Samsung bring to the game that Fokker couldn't by itself?"
Chi Sung-chul, an analyst at LG Securities, said: "The only demand we can see would be from the South Korean government for military use."

Samsung Group has deep pockets and great ambitions in aerospace. But not until a proposed multi-million dollar joint manufacturing deal with China fell apart did analysts believe Samsung would make a serious pitch for Fokker.
"The Sino-Korean project to build 100-seat passenger jets could have been a lucrative deal for Samsung," said Nam. "The deal would have secured a vast market -- China."
